extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, patent drafters, and patent attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent applications and evaluating patentability under common international/regional regimes (novelty, inventive step, utility, subject-matter eligibility, and disclosure). Focused on practical legal standards and drafting implications across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable, an invention must fulfill several requirements that are broadly classified as novelty, inventive step (nonobviousness) and industrial applicability (utility); additionally the claimed subject matter must be eligible for patent protection under the relevant national/regional law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All elements must be present in the single reference for lack of novelty; subject-matter eligibility is a threshold that gates further assessment of novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty generally requires that the claimed invention must not have been 'made available to the public' before the filing (or priority) date; lack of novelty (anticipation) occurs when all elements/features of a claim are found in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at least one feature in the claimed invention is not in the single prior art reference, the claim may be novel. Example: a rocking chair claim that omits rocker attachments can be anticipated by a prior chair with four legs if the claimed elements match exactly. Avoid public disclosure before filing; use NDAs to preserve novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Made available to the public" (definition for prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is 'made available to the public' if knowledge of it was shared with or accessible to any member of the public who is free to disclose the knowledge to others; it is not necessary that anyone actually read the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art can be oral, publication, use, display, exhibitions, social media, or online content. The standard focuses on availability/accessibility, not actual awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical scope and form of prior disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope of prior art may vary by jurisdiction; in many countries, a public disclosure anywhere in the world is valid prior art and prior art can take any form (oral, publication, use, display, exhibitions, social media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking protection in multiple countries, file before any disclosure because some countries have limited grace periods or narrow exceptions (e.g., EPC/China limited exceptions for exhibitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-filed, later-published patent applications (secret prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed in the same country before the filing (or priority) date but published only thereafter may become part of the prior art (secret or fictive prior art); treatment differs by jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example jurisdictional differences: Europe and Japan consider such applications for novelty only; the U.S. considers them for novelty and inventive step; in the U.S. and Japan they count only if filed by a third party, while Europe and China may include same-inventor filings as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period (nonprejudicial disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries provide a limited grace period during which an inventor’s own disclosure will not count as prior art (nonprejudicial); the type and duration of disclosures covered vary by jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: United States and Japan: comprehensive one-year grace period covering any disclosure by the inventor. Europe and China: very limited exceptions (e.g., disclosures at international exhibitions). Best practice: file before any public disclosure when seeking multi-country protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific claim scope (novelty implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a generic concept and prior art discloses a specific example included in that generic concept, the prior art can destroy novelty; conversely, a claim to a specific concept may remain novel against prior art only disclosing a broader generic concept if the specific has distinguishing technical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claim to 'conductive material' is anticipated by prior disclosure of 'copper material'; claim to 'copper material' may still be novel against prior disclosure of 'conductive material' if copper has distinguishing technical features (e.g., specific conductivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / Nonobviousness (principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step requires the invention not be obvious to a 'person skilled in the art' — i.e., an invention is nonobvious if an ordinarily skilled practitioner could not combine known information to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness can be found even if no single prior art reference discloses the invention, by combining multiple references. The requirement ensures the invention contributes an appropriate level of improvement to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis steps for inventive step (common approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical analysis involves determining: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claimed invention; and (3) the level of skill of those in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully compare claimed steps/features and prior art disclosures. If a person skilled in the art could obviously arrive at the claimed invention from the prior art, the invention is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution approach (EPO-style inventive step analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem–solution approach involves: (1) determining the closest prior art; (2) establishing distinguishing features between the claimed invention and that prior art; (3) formulating the objective technical problem; and (4) considering whether the claimed solution would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structured approach is commonly used by the EPO and useful for framing inventive-step arguments and claim drafting to highlight technical effects and inventive contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (hypothetical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical person presumed to have access to all publicly available prior art and have ordinary practical skills and general knowledge in the field, plus routine experimental capacity, but not inventive capabilities beyond logical combination of known information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes the skilled person is a team of specialists (e.g., biotech + IT for bioinformatics inventions). Do not attribute inventive imagination to this person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible hindsight analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex post facto or hindsight analysis — using knowledge of the invention to render it obvious — must be avoided when determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and courts should not let the inventor’s success bias the obviousness assessment; structure the analysis to avoid reading the invention back into the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that explicitly excludes or discourages an element may 'teach away' from that element and thus cannot be used to show obviousness against an invention containing that element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a prior disclosure excludes sulfuric acid from a copper electroplating solution; inventor’s successful use of sulfuric acid may support nonobviousness because the prior art taught away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective indicia of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as solving a long‑standing problem, overcoming previous failures by others, or commercial success can be considered as evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors may support inventive-step arguments, but they usually will not overcome a clear primary obviousness finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial application / Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be useful (utility) or have industrial application — typically meaning it performs the specified functions and achieves some minimally beneficial result; commercial viability is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions contrary to well-established physical laws (e.g., perpetual motion machines) are excluded. In life sciences, demonstration of effect in lab animals or a use as an intermediate can sometimes suffice. Ask: 'Are the results useful?' when deciding whether to file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter / Eligibility (threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter eligibility determines whether claimed subject matter falls within statutory categories (varies by jurisdiction) or whether it is excluded (laws of nature, abstract ideas, natural phenomena, etc.); only if eligible should novelty/inventive-step be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S.: positive statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) but subject-matter limits developed by case law (law of nature, abstract idea, natural phenomenon). Japan: 'creation of a technical idea utilizing a law of nature.' EPC and others list nonpatentable examples rather than a positive definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpatentable categories and the "as such" qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Many regimes exclude items such as discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, mental acts, games, business methods, computer programs, and presentations of information — but only if claimed 'as such'; the 'technical character' test is often used to distinguish patentable implementations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel inventive method of presenting information or a technical implementation of a computer program may be eligible even if the abstract content or program 'as such' is excluded. The EPO uses technical character jurisprudence to draw the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-specific exclusions (e.g., medical methods, plants, biological processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions exclude inventions for ordre public/morality reasons, diagnostic/therapeutic/surgical methods for humans/animals, and plants/animals (other than microorganisms) or essentially biological processes, though products for use in such treatments may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note differences: in some countries methods of treatment are excluded; in the U.S. they may be patentable but the patentee may be unable to enforce against a medical practitioner. Tailor filings to jurisdictional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement (purpose and components)
rubrics_metrics.description: In exchange for exclusive rights, patent applicants must sufficiently disclose the invention so the public can practice it after patent expiry; disclosure requirements typically include support/written description, enablement, and clarity, and in some countries a best mode requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure ensures the claims are justified by the description and prevents adding new subject matter after filing. Poor initial drafting can preclude later amendment to add needed disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement / Written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by the description (written description requirement in the U.S.): there must be a basis in the description for every claim and the scope of claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is supported unless a person skilled in the art would be unable, based on the application as filed, to extend the teaching of the description to the whole claimed field. Draft descriptions to underpin all claim scope you may later pursue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention without undue experimentation (enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is tied to the disclosure and varies by technology area; for complex biotech or chemical inventions, sufficient experimental detail or representative examples may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure and claims must be clear so that the scope of protection is communicated to others (clarity requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity problems can lead to rejections or limit enforceability. Draft claims and descriptions with precise language and avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (where applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries, applicants must disclose the best mode known to the inventor for carrying out the invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement affects drafting strategy: where applicable, include the preferred implementation known to the inventor to avoid later challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements and improvement patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are often granted for improvements on prior inventions; an improvement patent covers an enhanced effect compared with an earlier patent but may still require consent (license) from the earlier patent owner to practice if the earlier patent's claims cover the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Inventor B patents a faster, less-spill filling apparatus; if Inventor A's claims cover B's apparatus, B must license A to practice. Improvement patents are new patents and licensing negotiations are common; assess freedom-to-operate and potential blocking patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are territorial rights: protection is obtained on a country-by-country basis, so a patent granted in one country does not by itself prevent manufacturing or selling in other countries where no patent is held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking international protection, file in relevant jurisdictions because territorial scope affects enforcement and exploitation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent exploitation models and strategic uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can be exploited for revenue (licensing, royalties), marketing (patent marking), bargaining chips (cross-licensing), industry influence (blocking patents, essential patents to standards), and defensive purposes (prevent copying, create prior art, defend against litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic patenting choices (offensive vs defensive) have cost implications; consider portfolio strategy, cross-licensing potential, marking requirements, and antitrust/competition law risk where patents confer dominant positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive patenting (three senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'defensive patenting' can mean: (1) using patents to prevent competitors from copying products or to create prior art; (2) using patents to defend the company when sued; or (3) an inadequate/underfunded patent program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strategically defensive program can still be expensive; understand which sense applies when planning filings and budgets.
